city.name: London — East End
city.subtitle: Synagogues, migration, resistance and refuge
city.description: Walk from the City into Spitalfields and Whitechapel through places shaped by Sephardi worship, Ashkenazi immigration, anti-fascism and child refugees.

tour.title: Jewish East London: Synagogues, Migration and Resistance
tour.subtitle: Five sites spanning three centuries of Jewish London
tour.overview: A compact walking route connecting Britain's oldest continuously used synagogue with East End immigrant congregations, a preserved former synagogue, the Battle of Cable Street and the Kindertransport memorial.

stops.title: Bevis Marks Synagogue
stops.address: 12–16 Bevis Marks, London EC3A 7LH, United Kingdom
stops.shortDescription: The 1701 Spanish and Portuguese synagogue, the oldest synagogue in Britain in continuous regular use.
stops.fullDescription: Opened in 1701 for London's Spanish and Portuguese Jewish community, Bevis Marks preserves a worship space modelled on the Amsterdam Esnoga. Its continued use, furnishings and records make it central to British Sephardi heritage. Entry is controlled and visitors should book or check current arrangements.
stops.transcript: Bevis Marks Synagogue opened in 1701, only a few decades after Jews were readmitted to England. Its founders belonged to the Spanish and Portuguese Jewish community, many descended from families who had lived under the pressure of the Iberian Inquisition. The interior follows the Sephardi tradition, with the ark and reader's platform facing one another across a dignified, candle-lit room. Some benches and fittings date from the synagogue's earliest years. The building survived wartime bombing nearby and remains a place of prayer, not a reconstructed museum. Its secluded courtyard also reflects an earlier age when Jewish institutions were present but visually discreet. As you begin the tour, notice that East London's Jewish story did not start with nineteenth-century migration from Eastern Europe. Sephardi merchants, families and congregations established an enduring communal foundation. Check visiting times, security requirements and dress guidance before entering, and remember that continuity here depends on active worship as well as conservation.

stops.title: Sandys Row Synagogue
stops.address: 4A Sandys Row, London E1 7HW, United Kingdom
stops.shortDescription: An East End Ashkenazi congregation established by Dutch Jewish cigar makers in a converted Huguenot chapel.
stops.fullDescription: Sandys Row was founded in 1854 by Dutch Ashkenazi immigrants and moved into this former Huguenot chapel in 1867. The adapted building illustrates the layered migrant history of Spitalfields and the institutions Jewish workers created around worship, mutual help and burial.
stops.transcript: Sandys Row Synagogue grew from the lives of working immigrants. Dutch Ashkenazi Jews, many employed in cigar making, founded the congregation in 1854. In 1867 they acquired this building, originally constructed as a Huguenot chapel a century earlier and later used by other Christian groups. Turning it into a synagogue placed Jewish worship inside a structure already shaped by migration. Members organised more than prayer: congregations offered friendship, charity, burial arrangements and practical support in an unfamiliar city. The building's modest entrance contrasts with its warm interior and curved ark wall. Unlike many East End synagogues that closed as Jewish families moved to other parts of London, Sandys Row survived as a congregation and heritage site. That continuity is fragile and depends on volunteers, worshippers and conservation. If the building is closed, the exterior still tells a layered story: one immigrant community inherited and transformed the sacred space of another while making Spitalfields its home.

image.creator: Paul the Archivist
image.attributionText: Sandys Row Synagogue interior — Paul the Archivist, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.title: 19 Princelet Street
stops.address: 19 Princelet Street, London E1 6QH, United Kingdom
stops.shortDescription: An eighteenth-century immigrant house with an 1870 synagogue built into its garden.
stops.fullDescription: This 1719 Huguenot house later became home to Jewish immigrants. In 1870 a synagogue was constructed behind it for a congregation including migrants from Eastern Europe. Preserved as the Museum of Immigration and Diversity, the fragile building opens only on limited occasions; the tour must not promise entry.
stops.transcript: Number 19 Princelet Street looks like a Georgian house, but behind it stands a synagogue built in 1870. The house itself was constructed in 1719 for a Huguenot family, then adapted by later residents as Spitalfields changed. Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe crowded into the surrounding streets during the nineteenth century, and a congregation created its prayer hall in the garden. The building therefore compresses several migrations into one address. Its worn surfaces are part of the evidence: domestic rooms, workshop life and religious space overlap rather than appearing as separate museum displays. Today the Museum of Immigration and Diversity protects the property, but its physical fragility means public openings are rare. Do not expect or attempt entry unless an official event is advertised. From the street, consider how migration alters existing buildings and how communities inherit one another's neighbourhoods. The Jewish chapter belongs within a broader history of people seeking safety, work and belonging in London's East End.

stops.title: Cable Street and the Battle of Cable Street
stops.address: 236 Cable Street, London E1 0BL, United Kingdom
stops.shortDescription: A mural commemorating the 1936 mobilisation that blocked Oswald Mosley's fascists from marching through the East End.
stops.fullDescription: On 4 October 1936, Jewish residents, trade unionists, socialists, communists, Irish dockers and other East Enders resisted a planned British Union of Fascists march. The mural beside the former town hall commemorates the confrontation and the slogan ‘They shall not pass.’ Interpretation should acknowledge both collective solidarity and continuing debate over participants and policing.
stops.transcript: The Cable Street mural remembers 4 October 1936, when Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists planned to march through an East End with a large Jewish population. Residents and anti-fascist organisers built barricades and gathered in great numbers, while police attempted to clear a route for the march. Jewish groups, trade unionists, socialists, communists, Irish dockers and many neighbours took part. Mosley was eventually ordered to abandon the procession. The event became known as the Battle of Cable Street and the words ‘They shall not pass’ entered local memory. The mural, begun decades later, turns the street into a crowded visual narrative rather than presenting a single hero. It should not simplify the history: organisations disagreed about tactics, police and protesters clashed, and antisemitism did not disappear after one day. Yet Cable Street remains a powerful example of a threatened community and its allies asserting that fascist intimidation would not control their neighbourhood.

image.creator: Jon Hardy
image.attributionText: Cable Street Mural — Jon Hardy, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.title: Kindertransport Memorial — The Arrival
stops.address: Liverpool Street Station, Hope Square, London EC2M 7QH, United Kingdom
stops.shortDescription: Frank Meisler's sculpture remembering children who arrived in Britain through the Kindertransport rescue.
stops.fullDescription: The memorial outside Liverpool Street Station recalls nearly 10,000 mostly Jewish children brought from Nazi-controlled Europe to Britain between December 1938 and September 1939. Many arrived at this station and were met by sponsors or foster families. Rescue brought safety but also separation, loss and uncertain futures.
stops.transcript: These figures represent children arriving with luggage but without the families and certainty that should accompany childhood. Between December 1938 and the outbreak of war in September 1939, the Kindertransport brought nearly ten thousand children from Nazi-controlled Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland to Britain. Most were Jewish. Liverpool Street was a major arrival point, where children met sponsors, foster parents or representatives of hostels and schools. The scheme saved lives, but it also depended on parents making unbearable decisions. Many children never saw their families again. Sculptor Frank Meisler was himself a Kindertransport child, giving the memorial a personal link to the history it represents. Look at the different gestures and expressions rather than imagining one uniform experience. Some children found loving homes; others encountered loneliness, exploitation or repeated moves. The monument honours rescue while leaving space for separation and grief—the complex emotional inheritance carried by survivors and their descendants.

image.creator: Matt Brown
image.attributionText: Kindertransport — The Arrival — Matt Brown, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
